questions.stem:
An experiment consists of selecting a ball from a bag and spinning a coin. The bag contains 5 red balls and 7 blue balls. A ball is selected at random from the bag, its colour is noted and then the ball is returned to the bag.

When a red ball is selected, a biased coin with probability $\frac{2}{3}$ of landing heads is spun.

When a blue ball is selected a fair coin is spun.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Complete the tree diagram below to show the possible outcomes and associated probabilities.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: probabilities on the 1st two branches, P(R) and P(B). B1: 2nd set of probabilities.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- 1st B1 for the probabilities on the first 2 branches. Accept $0.41\dot{6}$ and $0.58\dot{3}$
- 2nd B1 for probabilities on the second set of branches. Accept $0.\dot{6}$, $0.\dot{3}$, 0.5 and $\frac{1.5}{3}$
- Allow exact decimal equivalents using clear recurring notation if required.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Shivani selects a ball and spins the appropriate coin.
(b) Find the probability that she obtains a head.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (b) M1: $\mathrm{P}(H) = \frac{5}{12}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{7}{12}\times\frac{1}{2}$, for an expression for P(H) that follows through their sum of two products of probabilities from their tree diagram. A1: $=\frac{41}{72}$ or awrt 0.569

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given that Tom selected a ball at random and obtained a head when he spun the appropriate coin,
(c) find the probability that Tom selected a red ball.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: (c) M1: $\mathrm{P}(R|H) = \dfrac{\frac{5}{12}\times\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{41}{72}}$ (formula seen, with denominator their (b) substituted, award M1; if formula not seen, M1 for probability times probability over their b, but M0 if fraction repeated). A1ft: for a fully correct expression or correct follow through. A1: $=\frac{20}{41}$ or awrt 0.488 o.e.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Shivani and Tom each repeat this experiment.
(d) Find the probability that the colour of the ball Shivani selects is the same as the colour of the ball Tom selects.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: (d) M1: $\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^2+\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)^2$, can follow through their equivalent values from tree diagram. A1ft: for both values correct or follow through from their original tree, and + . A1: $=\frac{25}{144}+\frac{49}{144}=\frac{74}{144}$ or $\frac{37}{72}$ or awrt 0.514, for a correct answer. Special Case: $\frac{5}{12}\times\frac{4}{11}+\frac{7}{12}\times\frac{6}{11}$ seen award M1A0A0

questions.stem:
The Venn diagram in Figure 1 shows the number of students in a class who read any of 3 popular magazines $A$, $B$ and $C$.

Figure 1

One of these students is selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that the probability that the student reads more than one magazine is $\frac{1}{6}$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) M1: $\frac{2+3}{\text{their total}}$ or $\frac{5}{30}$. A1cso: $=\frac{5}{\text{their total}}=\frac{1}{6}$ (given answer)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the probability that the student reads $A$ or $B$ (or both).
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (b) M1: for adding at least 3 of "4, 2, 5, 3" and dividing by their total to give a probability. Can be written as separate fractions substituted into the completely correct Addition Rule. A1: $\frac{4+2+5+3}{\text{total}}=\frac{14}{30}$ or $\frac{7}{15}$ or 0.46\.dot{6}

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Write down the probability that the student reads both $A$ and $C$.
(1)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Given that the student reads at least one of the magazines,
(d) find the probability that the student reads $C$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (d) M1: for a denominator of 20 or $\frac{20}{30}$ leading to an answer with denominator of 20; $\mathrm{P}(C|\text{reads at least one magazine})=\frac{6+3}{20}$. A1: $=\frac{9}{20}$ only, 2/2

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Determine whether or not reading magazine $B$ and reading magazine $C$ are statistically independent.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: (e) M1: attempting all the required probabilities for a suitable test: $\mathrm{P}(B)=\frac{10}{30}=\frac{1}{3}$, $\mathrm{P}(C)=\frac{9}{30}=\frac{3}{10}$, $\mathrm{P}(B\cap C)=\frac{3}{30}=\frac{1}{10}$ or $\mathrm{P}(B|C)=\frac{3}{9}$. M1: for use of a correct test - must have attempted all the correct probabilities. Equality can be implied in line 2: $\mathrm{P}(B)\times\mathrm{P}(C)=\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{3}{10}=\frac{1}{10}=\mathrm{P}(B\cap C)$ or $\mathrm{P}(B|C)=\frac{3}{9}=\frac{1}{3}=\mathrm{P}(B)$. A1cso: for fully correct test carried out with a comment - So yes they are statistically independent

questions.stem:
A teacher selects a random sample of 56 students and records, to the nearest hour, the time spent watching television in a particular week.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Hours} & 1-10 & 11-20 & 21-25 & 26-30 & 31-40 & 41-59\\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 6 & 15 & 11 & 13 & 8 & 3\\ \hline \text{Mid-point} & 5.5 & 15.5 & & 28 & & 50\\ \hline\end{array}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the mid-points of the $21-25$ hour and $31-40$ hour groups.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) B1: 23 B1: 35.5 (may be in the table)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A histogram was drawn to represent these data. The $11-20$ group was represented by a bar of width $4\,\text{cm}$ and height $6\,\text{cm}$.
(b) Find the width and height of the $26-30$ group.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: (b) B1: Width of 10 units is $4\,\text{cm}$ so width of 5 units is $2\,\text{cm}$. M1: their width $\times$ their height $= 20.8$; height $=2.6\times4$. A1: $=10.4\,\text{cm}$. Without labels assume width first, height second and award marks accordingly.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Estimate the mean and standard deviation of the time spent watching television by these students.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: reasonable attempt at $\sum x$ and $/56$; $\sum fx = 1316.5 \Rightarrow \bar{x}=\frac{1316.5}{56}$. A1: awrt 23.5. B1: $\sum fx^2 = 37378.25$ can be implied. M1: a method for $\sigma$ or $s$, square root required; $\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{37378.25}{56}-\bar{x}^2}$. A1: awrt 10.7 allow $s=10.8$. Typical errors: $\sum (fx)^2 = 354806.3$ M0, $\sum f^2x = 13922.5$ M0 and $\left(\sum fx\right)^2 = 1733172$ M0.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Correct answers only, award full marks.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median length of time spent watching television by these students.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (d) M1: $Q_2=(20.5)+\frac{(28-21)}{11}\times5=23.68\ldots$. Use of $\sum f(x-\bar{x})^2 = $ awrt 6428.75 for B1. lcb can be 20, 20.5 or 21, width can be 4 or 5 and the fraction part of the formula correct for M1 - Allow 28.5 in fraction that gives awrt 23.9 for M1A1. A1: awrt 23.7 or 23.9

parts.label: e
parts.text:
The teacher estimated the lower quartile and the upper quartile of the time spent watching television to be 15.8 and 29.3 respectively.
(e) State, giving a reason, the skewness of these data.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (e) M1: for attempting a test for skewness using quartiles or mean and median; $Q_3-Q_2=5.6$, $Q_2-Q_1=7.9$ (or $\bar{x}<Q_2$). Provided median greater than 22.55 and less than 29.3 award for $Q_3-Q_2<Q_2-Q_1$ without values as a valid reason. A1: [7.9 > 5.6 so] negative skew. SC Accept mean close to median and no skew o.e. for M1A1

questions.stem: The distances travelled to work, $D$ km, by the employees at a large company are normally distributed with $D \sim \mathrm{N}(30, 8^2)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected employee has a journey to work of more than 20 km.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) M1: for an attempt to standardise 20 or 40 using 30 and 8; $\mathrm{P}(D>20)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{20-30}{8}\right)$. A1: $=\mathrm{P}(Z>-1.25)$, for $z=\pm1.25$. A1: $=0.8944$, awrt 0.894

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme: (b) M1: $\mathrm{P}(D<Q_3)=0.75$ so $\frac{Q_3-30}{8}=0.67$, for $\frac{Q_3-30}{8}=$ to a $z$ value; M0 for 0.7734 on RHS. B1: (z value) between 0.67~0.675 seen. A1: $Q_3=$ awrt 35.4. M1B0A1 for use of $z=0.68$ in correct expression with awrt 35.4

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Write down the lower quartile, $Q_1$, of $D$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (c) $35.4-30=5.4$ so $Q_1=30-5.4=$ awrt 24.6. B1ft: follow through using their of quartile values.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
An outlier is defined as any value of $D$ such that $D<h$ or $D>k$ where
$h = Q_1 - 1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$ and $k = Q_3+1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$
(d) Find the value of $h$ and the value of $k$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: (d) M1: $Q_3-Q_1=10.8$ so $1.5(Q_3-Q_1)=16.2$ so $Q_1-16.2=h$ or $Q_3+16.2=k$, for an attempt to calculate $1.5(IQR)$ and attempt to add or subtract using one of the formulae given in the question - follow through their quartiles. A1: $h=$ 8.4 to 8.6 and $k=$ 51.4 to 51.6, both

parts.label: e
parts.text:
An employee is selected at random.
(e) Find the probability that the distance travelled to work by this employee is an outlier.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: (e) M1: $2\mathrm{P}(D>51.6)=2\mathrm{P}(Z>2.7)$, for attempting $2\mathrm{P}(D>\text{their }k)$ or $(\mathrm{P}(D>\text{their }k)+\mathrm{P}(D<\text{their }h))$. M1: $=2[1-0.9965]$, for standardising their $h$ or $k$ (may have missed the 2) so allow for standardising $\mathrm{P}(D>51.6)$ or $\mathrm{P}(D<8.4)$; require both Ms to award A mark. A1: $=$ awrt 0.007
